newsitem.title: GERMANY: IW says higher incomes to boost German consumption.
newsitem.headline: IW says higher incomes to boost German consumption.

text.p: A boost in real incomes, low inflation and falling savings rates could help Germany overcome the current weakness in private consumption this year, the IW think tank said on Wednesday.

IW, one of Germany's six leading economic research institutes and a close affiliate of employers' groups, said private households will increase spending by 80 billion marks this year, boosting comsumption by a real 2.5 percent, after a 1.5 percent gain in 1996.

Higher personal consumption would be especially important for the German economy, as a one percent rise in private consumption would boost gross domestic product by 0.6 percent, twice as much as a similar rise in exports, it said.
An expected inflation rate of 1.5 percent in 1997 will be low enough to allow further rises in real incomes, which gained 4.4 percent between 1993 and 1996, IW said.
The Bundesbank has grounds to leave interest rates low, making credit purchases more attractive. And the savings rate is expected to fall to 11.3 percent from 11.6 percent, it said.
Consumers remain worried about the high level of payroll withholdings and unemployment, but 1997 should bring tax relief and higher government support for children.
In addition, the economic recovery should create new jobs and make existing jobs more secure, it said.
Separately, a poll by the financial magazine Boerse Online said only one-third of corporate directors expect German economic growth to exceed two percent this year.
Many of the 100 executives polled see growth continuing to come mainly from exports, as capital investment, private consumption and construction remain lacklustre.
